q: A colleague asks AI to “pick the best applicants.” What would be a better request?
options: Find quotes that match our scoring guide, show where each quote came from, and leave the decision to staff.
Rank applicants by how impressive they sound.
Use a longer request and tell AI to be fair.
why: Ask AI for something you can check. You can look up a quote in the original application. Staff still decide what it means and how to score it.

q: You remove names from applications. Is it now OK to upload them to your personal AI account?
options: Yes. Removing names hides who everyone is.
Ask your organization which AI account and information you are allowed to use.
Yes, as long as you delete the chat afterward.
why: A story, school name, or other detail may still identify someone. Check your organization’s rules before uploading anything. For this workshop, use the made-up practice files.

q: A17 is a made-up applicant code used instead of a name. A file list (called a manifest) includes A17-transcript.pdf. AI can see only the list, not the document. What can AI tell you?
options: The transcript meets the requirements.
The applicant qualifies for the scholarship.
The file name is on the list. A person must open the document to check it.
why: Seeing a file name is like seeing a book title in a catalog. It does not mean you have read the book. A17-transcript.pdf means the transcript file for the applicant called A17.

q: An application says “I ran 12 tutoring sessions.” AI adds “Grades improved by 20%.” The application never says that. What should you do?
options: Keep the extra detail because it sounds believable.
Remove the extra claim and check the rest against the application.
Keep it if AI says it is very confident.
why: AI added a fact that the application does not support. Remove it. Check the other details too, even if the answer sounds confident.

q: Two applicants describe doing the same work. One writes more smoothly. If you are scoring their community work, what should you do?
options: Give the same score for the same work, using the scoring guide.
Give more points to the smoother writer.
Average the two scores without checking them.
why: Score what this part of the guide asks about: the work they did. Better writing alone does not show a greater community contribution.
practice: Compare the two practice statements. A17 and A18 are made-up applicant codes.

q: A tool says an applicant’s essay may have been written by AI. What is the fairest next step?
options: Reject the application right away.
Assume essays the tool does not flag were written without AI.
Have staff check the concern under the published rules and give the applicant a chance to explain.
why: These tools can be wrong. A flag is a reason to look more closely, not proof of cheating. Staff should follow the rules applicants received and explain how someone can ask for another review.

q: A19 is a made-up applicant code used instead of a name. This applicant applied late and asked for extra time. Who should decide whether to allow it?
options: AI, as long as its answer is in a table.
A staff member, using the organization’s rules and keeping a record of the reason.
AI, as long as it reads the date correctly.
why: AI can point out the late date and the request for extra time. A person must check the situation and decide what the rules allow.

q: You save a set of instructions for AI to reuse. This is often called a skill. What should you do before trusting it?
options: Assume saved instructions always give correct answers.
Keep adding instructions without trying them.
Try it on made-up examples where you know the answer, then check and fix mistakes.
why: Saving instructions does not make them reliable. Try an easy example, one with missing information, and one with a misleading request inside it. Check what AI does before using the instructions again.
practice: See how to try a reusable skill.
